original_interpretation: Intel FY2025 10-K: discontinued planned Germany fab and Poland assembly/test expansions; slowed Ohio fab construction.
evidence_found: "slowed the pace of construction for our new Ohio wafer fabrication facility, or fab, and discontinued planned expansions in Germany (fab) and Poland (assembly and test facility)." (Intel 10-K for FY ended 27 Dec 2025, Business section; repeated in Manufacturing section)
notes: Opened the SEC EDGAR filing directly. Same passage says these actions were taken in 2025 alongside consolidating Costa Rica assembly/test into Vietnam and Malaysia.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020: US 10-yr fab TCO ~30% above Taiwan/S.Korea/Singapore and 37-50% above China.
evidence_found: "the ten-year total cost of ownership of a new fab located in the US is approximately 30% higher than in Taiwan, South Korea, or Singapore, and 37% to 50% higher than in China" (Executive Summary)
notes: Executive-summary wording; the body (p.18) gives 25-30% vs Taiwan/Singapore and ~50% vs China (CLM-2075). TCO is net of incentives (endnote 8: capex + 10 yrs cash opex minus incentives). BCG+SIA joint study; research_firm/tier 2 is reasonable.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020 body: US TCO ~25-30% above Taiwan or Singapore for all three fab types; ~50% above China.
evidence_found: "across all three types of fabs the TCO for a US-based fab is approximately 25% to 30% higher than the equivalent fab located in Taiwan or Singapore. (See Exhibit 7.) ... In the US, the TCO is roughly 50% higher than in China" (p. 18)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020: 40-70% of the US cost gap is directly attributable to government incentives.
evidence_found: "As much as 40% to 70% of that cost differential is directly attributable to government incentives." (Executive Summary); "Depending on the type of fab and the country in question, these incentives make up 40% to 70% of the cost advantage other countries have over the US." (p. 19)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020: annual cash opex of a new fab ~US$0.6-2.0bn.
evidence_found: "we calculate that the ongoing cash operating expenses (labor, utilities, and so on) amount to approxi- mately $0.6 billion to $2.0 billion per year." (p. 17)
notes: Metric population lists 'materials, taxes' and geography 'average across seven countries'; the source only says 'labor, utilities, and so on' and does not state the geography basis. Figure itself is correct.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020: gross 10-yr TCO before incentives US$11-15bn (analog), US$30-40bn (logic/memory).
evidence_found: "the total gross TCO of a new fab—without considering govern- ment incentives—over a ten-year period can reach a stag- gering $11 billion to $15 billion (for advanced analog) and $30 billion to $40 billion (for advanced logic or memory)." (p. 17)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020: incentives offset 15-40% of gross fab TCO depending on country.
evidence_found: "In total, we estimate that government incentives can offset be- tween 15% and 40% of the gross TCO (before incentives) of a new fab, depending on the country." (p. 17)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020 reference logic fab: 12-inch, 5nm, 35k wpm, ~3,000 staff, ~US$20bn capex.
evidence_found: Exhibit 5 (p. 17), Advanced Logic column: "12-inch wafer size • 5 nm node ... Capacity (wafers per month) 35,000 ... No. of employees ~3,000 ... Capital investment ($ billion) ~20" (Sources: SIA; BCG analysis)
notes: Table read from extracted PDF text; column order (logic, memory, analog) is consistent across all rows.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020 reference memory fab: 12-inch 128-layer 3D NAND, 100k wpm, ~6,000 staff, ~US$20bn capex.
evidence_found: Exhibit 5 (p. 17), Advanced Memory column: "3D NAND, 128 layers • 12-inch wafer size • 20 nm node"; "Capacity (wafers per month) ... 100,000"; "No. of employees ... ~6,000"; "Capital investment ($ billion) ... ~20"
notes: Exhibit also lists a 20 nm node for the memory fab, omitted from the claim.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG 2020 reference analog fab: 12-inch 65nm, 40k wpm, ~3,000 staff, ~US$5bn capex.
evidence_found: Exhibit 5 (p. 17), Advanced Analog column: "12-inch wafer size • 65 nm node"; capacity "40,000"; employees "~3,000"; capital investment "~5". p.17 text: "a state-of-the-art semiconductor fab of standard capacity requires roughly between $5 billion (for an advanced analog fab) and $20 billion (for advanced logic and memory fabs) of capital expenditure"
notes: Confirms the note that the 2020 report itself states the US$5-20bn range (consistent with CLM-0481).

original_interpretation: BCG 2023: greenfield 2nm-class logic fab completed in 2026 has 10-yr TCO US$35-43bn, 33-66% above today.
evidence_found: "we concluded that a fab completed in 2026 would carry a ten-year TCO of $35 billion to $43 billion—33% to 66% higher than today’s costs. (See Exhibit 5.)" (Cost of a Hypothetical Fab); fab defined as "a greenfield next-gen fab that would manufacture 2nm to sub-2nm nodes at 300-millimeter wafer size. Initial production would be scheduled for 2026."
notes: Also confirmed: "if the inflation rate ends up at 2.6% rather than 4%, the cost of building a fab in 2026 could drop to as low as $37 billon." A model estimate, not an actual cost.

original_interpretation: BCG 2023: US construction prices +6% CAGR since 2021; materials +25% CAGR.
evidence_found: "construction prices in the US have risen by a 6% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) since 2021, and materials costs have ballooned by 25% CAGR. (See Exhibit 3.)"
notes: End year is implicit (article dated 28 Sep 2023); the underlying index is not named in the text.

original_interpretation: BCG 2023 expects fab construction-cost inflation to stay above general inflation because of limited specialised talent after few recent US/European buildouts.
evidence_found: "We estimate that inflation in fab construction costs will continue to remain elevated compared with broader inflation levels, primarily because without a sustained volume of new fab buildouts in recent years in many geographies—such as the US and parts of Europe—there is a limited amount of talent and expertise to support such highly specialized building programs."
notes: Classification: this is BCG's sourced forecast, so claim_type should be 'estimate', not 'interpretation'. As recorded it is an interpretation, so confidence stays low under the rules.

original_interpretation: BCG 2023: leading-edge fab operating labour costs expected to be relatively stable (automation), while maintenance and materials costs rise.
evidence_found: "Perhaps surprisingly, operating labor costs are expected to be relatively stable. Leading-edge fabs are extensively automated ... staff size and responsibilities ... won’t need to change substantially. However, maintenance costs are expected to continue to rise"; materials: "greater amounts of materials will be needed for the additional layers and process steps" (Ongoing Expenses)

original_interpretation: BCG 2023: state/local taxes in NY, TX, AZ, OH, CA are 4-7% and 1-3% of 10-yr TCO.
evidence_found: "state and local taxes in US states that already have had some degree of semiconductor industry presence (such as New York, Texas, Arizona, Ohio, and California) range from 4% to 7% and account for 1% to 3% of the ten-year TCO."
notes: The five states are BCG's examples ('such as'), not an exhaustive list.

original_interpretation: CSET 2022 recommended US$5-10bn of CHIPS incentives for one large leading-edge DRAM fab and >=US$23bn for leading-edge logic.
evidence_found: "This brief recommends appropriating at least $23 billion (62 percent) of CHIPS Act incentives for leading-edge logic capacity." ... "An additional $5-10 billion should be used to incentivize the construction of one large leading-edge DRAM fab." (Executive Summary)
notes: CSET defines the DRAM fab as 100,000 WPM ('the minimum cost-effective DRAM footprint'). It is a policy recommendation, not an outcome.

original_interpretation: CSET: ~635 greenfield fabs built 1990-2020 took on average 682 days (~1.86 years) from construction start to production.
evidence_found: "Between 1990 and 2020 there were approximately 635 greenfield semiconductor fabs built around the world. The average time between the construction start date and the beginning date of production was 682 days or roughly 1.86 years." (p. 6); Figure 1 source: "World Fab Forecast. Sample consisted of 635 greenfield fab construction projects"
notes: Classification: this is CSET's analysis of SEMI World Fab Forecast data, so 'estimate' fits better than 'fact'. Read from the PDF text layer.

original_interpretation: CSET 1990-2020: Japan 584 days, Korea 620 days fastest; Americas 736 days; only SE Asia slower.
evidence_found: "As Figure 1 shows, Japan (584 days) and South Korea (620 days) build fabs significantly faster than the rest of the world on average. The Americas ... taking an average of 736 days, or roughly five months longer than Japan. Only construction of fabs in Southeast Asia takes longer than in the Americas." (p. 6)
notes: Figure 1 values 584, 620, 654, 690, 701, 736, 781 run in reverse of the axis labels (SE Asia ... Japan). That suggests Taiwan 654, Europe & Mideast 690, China 701, SE Asia 781, but this is inferred from chart order and not recorded as a claim.

original_interpretation: CSET 2021: in volume production, energy can be up to 30% of a fab's operating costs.
evidence_found: "Once a fab has reached volume production, energy costs can account for up to 30 percent of the fab’s operating costs.13" (p. 5)
notes: CSET cites this from a secondary source (endnote 13), so it is an upper bound, not a CSET model figure.

original_interpretation: CSET 2021: fab shells are 20-40% of greenfield fab capex.
evidence_found: "Fab “shells,” the physical structures that house semiconductor manufacturing equipment (SME) and all associated materials and supporting operations, can occupy hundreds of acres and account for between 20 and 40 percent of the total capital expenditures associated with a greenfield semiconductor manufacturing facility.6"

original_interpretation: CRS R46581 (2020): experts say a new fab costs at least US$7bn, up to US$20bn for advanced; much obsolete in 5-6 years.
evidence_found: "industry experts say that a new semiconductor factory, much of which may be obsolete after five or six years, now costs at least $7 billion to build, with some asserting that an advanced chip fab can cost as much as $20 billion.50" (identical in the EveryCRSReport mirror and the original CRS PDF)
notes: Checked against the original CRS PDF (crsreports.congress.gov) and added it to the claim's sources; the wording matches. Page number 'p. 12' not independently confirmed. It reports unnamed experts, so 'estimate' is correct.

original_interpretation: CRS 2020, citing one assessment: TSMC Arizona wafers at least 7% costlier than Taiwan/China; due to small capacity and higher construction, labour, utility costs.
evidence_found: "the wafers it produces are expected to be at least 7% more expensive to manufacture than if they were made in Taiwan or China, according to one assessment of the project. The differential is attributed to the planned facility’s relatively small capacity as well as to higher construction, labor, and utility costs.60"; fn 60: "Scotten Jones, 'Cost Analysis of the Proposed TSMC US Fab,' SemiWiki.com, May 15, 2020"
notes: Resolves the claim's note: footnote 60 is the IC Knowledge/SemiWiki article (SRC-0703). That article compares only to Fab 18 in Taiwan ('approximately 7%'); 'or China' and 'at least' are CRS's additions.

original_interpretation: IC Knowledge May 2020: US labour and utilities add ~3.4% to TSMC 5nm Arizona (20k wpm) wafer cost vs Taiwan.
evidence_found: "The fab will run TSMC’s 5nm technology and have a capacity of 20,000 wafers per month (wpm)." ... "Locating a fab in the US versus Taiwan will result in the fab incurring US labor and utility costs, this will add approximately 3.4% to the wafer manufacturing cost."
notes: Superseded by the author's own 2021 revision (CLM-2097: 7% country difference), which is already in the database; the 2020 figure is still correct as a historical estimate. Same article: +3.8% for 20k vs 30k wpm scale, ~1.3% for no GigaFab construction, total ~7% vs Fab 18.

original_interpretation: IC Knowledge 2020: GigaFab clustering of 6-7 fabs believed to cut construction cost ~25% vs a stand-alone fab.
evidence_found: "Fab 12, Fab 14, Fab 15 and Fab 18 are each made up of 6 or 7 wafers fabs sharing central facility plants. This Gigafab approach is believed to reduce construction costs by about 25% versus building a single stand-alone fab."
notes: The source hedges it as 'believed'; no method given.

original_interpretation: IC Knowledge 2021: TSMC Arizona wafer 7% costlier than Taiwan (same size), 17% incl. 20k vs 80k wpm scale and clustering.
evidence_found: "after accounting for all the operating cost differences, we now find a 7% increase in cost to operate in Arizona versus Taiwan." ... "accounting for a 20,000 wpm fab in the US versus 80,000 wpm in Taiwan, plus the efficiency of clustering multiple fabs together in Taiwan adds 10% to the country-to-country difference found in 1. For a total 17% difference."
notes: Figure is correct for the 2021 model. 80,000 wpm is the planned per-phase capacity of Fab 18 (then ~40,000). A newer estimate from the same model family (TechInsights 2025: 'less than 10%') is added as a new claim with an open contradiction record. Treat 17% as a 2021 estimate.

original_interpretation: IC Knowledge 2021: direct labour ~0.1% of TSMC Taiwan wafer cost; US rate >3x but still <1%; US utilities cheaper.
evidence_found: "direct labor cost in the US are over 3x the rate in Taiwan, but they have only minimal impact because in Taiwan direct labor is only 0.1% of the wafer cost and even tripling or quadrupling the labor rate it is still less than 1% of the wafer cost. Utility costs are the other hand are lower in the US."

original_interpretation: IC Knowledge models depreciate equipment/installs/automation over 5 years, building systems 10, building 15, matching common reporting lives.
evidence_found: "The equipment, equipment installs, and automation are then depreciated over five years, the building systems over ten years and the building over fifteen years. We use these default values because most companies use these lifetimes for reporting purpose."
notes: Classification: a firm describing its own model and asserting what 'most companies' do is better typed 'reported_claim' than 'fact'.

original_interpretation: IC Knowledge 2021, 24 countries: labour rates 21x, engineer salaries 12x, electricity 2.8x, gas 7.6x spread.
evidence_found: "DL rates by country and year for 24 countries. In 2021 the difference in labor rate from the least expensive to most expensive country was 21x!"; "Difference in engineer salaries vary by 12x"; "Electrical rates vary by 2.8x by country and natural gas by 7.6x by country"
notes: Only the labour figure is explicitly dated 2021; the others come from the same October 2021 article.

original_interpretation: Hutcheson 2025: 150% is a rule of thumb for a first fab at a new site with unskilled labour; most published Arizona-vs-Taiwan comparisons overstated the gap.
evidence_found: "But 150% is a general rule of thumb for building the first fab at a new site with a new, unskilled, labor force… Pundits clearly didn’t understand the nuances of wafer costs"; "it was clear most pundits had no clue as to the actual cost difference"; "The final answer was: It costs TSMC less than 10% more to process a 300mm wafer in Arizona"
notes: Typed 'interpretation', but it is a sourced statement by TechInsights, so 'reported_claim' or 'estimate' would be more accurate. Its key number (<10% Arizona premium) was not recorded, so it is added as a new claim along with labour <2% and equipment >2/3 of wafer cost. This is a public blog summary of a paywalled analysis.

original_interpretation: TSMC Apr 2025: 1Q25 GM 58.8% included start of Kumamoto dilution; FY2025 overseas dilution forecast 2-3%.
evidence_found: "our first quarter gross margin slightly decreased by 20 basis points sequentially to 58.8%. This was primarily due to 60 basis points impact from the January 21 earthquake ... as well as the start of dilution from our Kumamoto fab ... forecast 2% to 3% margin dilution impact for the full year 2025." (TSMC IR 1Q25 transcript, CFO key messages)
notes: Checked the TickerTrends mirror against TSMC's own IR transcript; the wording matches, and the original was added to the claim's sources. FY2025 guidance was later cut to 1-2% (CLM-2106) and should be read as April 2025 guidance.

original_interpretation: TSMC: under fragmented globalization, overseas fab costs are higher for everyone including TSMC.
evidence_found: "As we have said before, under today's fragmented globalization environment, overseas fab costs are higher for everyone, including TSMC and all other semiconductor manufacturers." (TSMC IR 1Q25 transcript, 17 Apr 2025)
notes: Company view, correctly typed reported_claim. Original IR transcript added as source.

original_interpretation: TSMC Oct 2025 cut FY2025 overseas dilution to 1-2% (from 2-3%) citing scale; ~2% in 2H25.
evidence_found: "While the cost of overseas fabs remain higher, thanks to the company's overall larger scale, we now expect the gross margin dilution from the ramp-up of our overseas fabs to be closer to 2% in the second half of 2025. For the full year 2025, we now expect it to be between 1% to 2% as compared to 2% to 3% previously." (TSMC IR 3Q25 transcript, 16 Oct 2025)
notes: Mirror matches the original IR transcript, which was added as a source.

original_interpretation: TSMC: overseas-fab dilution 2-3% early, widening to 3-4% later over next several years; repeated Jan and Apr 2026.
evidence_found: 4Q25 (15 Jan 2026, IR transcript): "we continue to forecast the margin dilution from the ramp-up of overseas fabs in the next several years to be between 2% to 3% in the early stages and widen to 3% to 4% in the latter stages." 1Q26 (16 Apr 2026, IR transcript): "2% to 3% in the early stages and widen to 3% to 4% in the latter stages." Also on the 3Q25 call and on the 2Q26 call (16 Jul 2026).
notes: Checked against TSMC IR transcripts for 3Q25, 4Q25 (SRC-0025), 1Q26 and 2Q26; the guidance is unchanged through July 2026. April 2025 version: 'in the next five years to start from 2% to 3% every year in the early stages and widened to 3% to 4%'. SRC-0709 (TrendForce) paraphrases ('2%-3% in the near term ... 3%-4% over time').

original_interpretation: TSMC expects initial 2nm ramp to dilute FY2026 gross margin by 2-3%.
evidence_found: Jan 2026 (4Q25 IR transcript): "the initial ramp-up of our two-nanometer technology will start to dilute our gross margin in the second half of the year, and we expect between 2% to 3% dilution for the full year of 2026." Repeated Apr 2026 (1Q26). July 2026 (2Q26 IR transcript): "we expect a steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer to dilute our gross margin by about 3 to 4 percentage points in the second half of the year."
correction: Superseded by July 2026 guidance: 2nm ramp to dilute gross margin by about 3-4 percentage points in 2H2026 (new claim, supersedes CLM-2108). Label the 2-3% FY2026 figure as Jan/Apr 2026 guidance.
notes: Accurate as January/April 2026 guidance (now re-pointed to the IR transcripts). In July 2026 TSMC re-framed it as 3-4 points of dilution in 2H26 because of a 'steep' ramp, and did not restate a full-year figure.

original_interpretation: TSMC: capex per 1k wpm of N2 substantially higher than N3; A14 higher still; no figures.
evidence_found: "the CapEx dollar required to build 1k wafer-per-month capacity of N2 is substantially higher than 1k wafer-per-month capacity for N3. The CapEx-per-k cost for A14 will be even higher (added by company after the call)." (TSMC IR 4Q25 transcript, 15 Jan 2026, p. 4)
notes: The official IR transcript marks the A14 sentence as 'added by company after the call', so it is a written company addition, not something spoken on the call. The mirror omits that marker. Still a TSMC statement.
